docs.title: Water stress threatens wheat acreage as farmers eye better-paying rabi crops
docs.text:
This winter, wheat growers are weighing a harder choice than usual: plant a crop that needs water they may not have, or move to rabi options that promise better returns. The shift could trim India’s wheat acreage by 5 to 10 per cent, but the market may not feel the pinch immediately because government stocks remain comfortably above prescribed norms. 
 Water stress is reshaping planting decisions 
Farmers in Rajasthan, Gujarat and parts of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra are expected to cut back on wheat sowing after a weak monsoon left irrigation systems under strain, industry executives said. In several pockets, the shortage is so acute that growers may leave land fallow rather than commit to a crop that depends on assured water at the time of sowing and early growth. 
 That concern is not limited to one region. The pressure is spreading across key wheat belts as reservoirs, canals and local water sources fail to recover adequately from the monsoon deficit. The result is a more cautious approach to rabi planting, with farmers increasingly comparing water needs, input costs and expected returns before deciding what to sow. 
 Lower support price gains are weakening wheat’s pull 
A second factor is making wheat less attractive. The increase in the minimum support price for wheat was below 1 per cent, the smallest rise among major rabi crops , according to Navneet Chitlangia , president of the Roller Flour Millers’ Federation of India. He said the modest revision is unlikely to do much to encourage farmers already facing higher water risk and stronger price signals from competing crops. 
 Chitlangia added that the government’s broader policy push is also nudging growers towards oilseeds and pulses, which are central to India’s self-sufficiency goals. For farmers, however, the immediate calculation is simpler: if mustard, chana or maize can fetch more than wheat, and require less water, the incentive to switch becomes difficult to ignore. 
 Rohi Khaitan , a wheat processor from West Bengal, said the price gap between wheat and other rabi crops is wide enough to influence planting choices this season. He expects many growers to move away from wheat because prevailing prices for chana, mustard and maize are significantly higher than those of the cereal. 
 Some states are already urging a crop shift 
State governments are responding to the water squeeze with cautionary advice. Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh have begun telling farmers to choose crops that need less irrigation, reflecting the growing concern that a poor water year could reduce both the area sown and the productivity of whatever is planted. 
The situation is more severe in parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka and Telangana, where local politicians say some farmers may be unable to sow any rabi crop at all. In those areas, the issue is no longer just about switching from wheat to another crop, but about whether cultivation can proceed at all in the current season. 
 This creates a familiar policy tension. On one hand, lower water use and a move towards pulses and oilseeds align with national agricultural priorities. On the other, a sharp reduction in wheat acreage could unsettle growers, millers and local markets if supplies tighten more quickly than expected. 
 Why prices may stay contained despite lower output 
For now, the milling industry believes the supply side is strong enough to absorb a moderate decline in sowing. Chitlangia said wheat held by the Food Corporation of India is almost twice the buffer requirement, giving the government enough stock to manage market supply and prevent a sudden price spike. 
 That stock cushion has already had wider consequences. India has been able to export an estimated 300,000 tonnes of wheat after lifting a four-year ban on overseas shipments, a sign that available inventories are plentiful enough to support limited trade without endangering domestic supply. 
The Food Corporation of India has also opened its first tender of 2026 under the open market sales scheme, a mechanism used to release grain into the market when supplies are abundant. Such sales typically help moderate retail prices and reduce the burden on government warehouses by moving excess wheat into private channels. 
 What the coming months could mean for the wheat market 
The immediate outlook is therefore mixed. On the production side, wheat sowing may fall as water scarcity , weak price incentives and competition from better-paying crops all pull farmers in different directions. On the market side, large public stocks and continuing government sales should keep a lid on volatility, at least in the near term. 
That balance could change later if the acreage decline turns out to be deeper than expected or if weather conditions worsen further. For now, the more likely outcome is a smaller wheat crop, a larger shift towards alternative rabi crops and a market that stays relatively stable because the state is still sitting on ample grain reserves.

docs.title: Bihar clamps down on non-subsidised fertiliser sales, raising access concerns
docs.text:
Bihar ’s latest fertiliser order has reopened a familiar debate in the sector: how far can governments go in stopping bundling practices without narrowing farmers’ access to newer crop nutrition products? 
The state has joined Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh in restricting the sale of non-subsidised fertilisers by companies that also supply government-backed products such as urea , di-ammonium phosphate , NPK complexes and muriate of potash . Industry executives say the move may curb tagging, but it could also shrink the range of inputs available through the same dealer network that farmers already use for their seasonal purchases. 
 Why the industry is worried 
The immediate concern for manufacturers is not only distribution, but also economics. Companies that sell specialty fertilisers, micronutrients and other crop nutrition products alongside conventional subsidised products could lose as much as ₹120 crore in margins, according to industry estimates. The hit, executives say, would come at a time when the sector is trying to push more efficient nutrient use and persuade farmers to move beyond a narrow fertiliser mix. 
 Unlike subsidised fertilisers, which are sold at retail prices supported or controlled by the government, non-subsidised products are priced by the market. That difference matters because many companies have built their sales strategy around offering both categories through the same sales channels. If the non-subsidised portfolio is cut off from those channels, firms say they may struggle to expand the use of newer products designed to improve yields and soil health. 
 What the Bihar order targets 
The restrictions are intended to stop tagging, an industry practice in which dealers or suppliers tie the purchase of non-subsidised fertilisers to access to subsidised stocks. Officials and companies familiar with the issue say the practice can distort buying behaviour and force farmers into taking products they did not plan to buy. On paper, the Bihar order is aimed at cleaning up that market behaviour. 
 But the industry argues that the policy may end up being broader than the problem it seeks to solve. In a joint l et ter dated October 9, several major fertiliser players asked the Bihar government to reconsider the directive, saying it could limit access to essential nutrients and weaken soil health and crop productivity. The letter, which ET has seen, also flagged Bihar’s low soil organic carbon levels, arguing that balanced nutrient application is especially important in the state. 
 Fertiliser makers see a wider operational risk 
Executives say the impact may not stop at sales loss. One senior official at a large fertiliser manufacturer that sells both subsidised and non-subsidised products said the order could discourage investment in crop nutrition technologies that are meant to improve fertiliser-use efficiency. The same official added that the restrictions may also disrupt manufacturing operations for organic and sulphur-based products, while affecting supplies routed through dealers operating under the government’s one-stop fertiliser outlet model. 
That concern reflects a broader industry shift. Over the past few years, fertiliser companies have been trying to reposition themselves not just as sellers of bulk nutrients, but as providers of a wider crop nutrition basket that includes speciality formulations and micronutrient blends. The Bihar move, executives say, risks separating the subsidised and non-subsidised parts of that business at the very point where companies are trying to integrate them for farmers. 
 A policy trade-off already seen elsewhere 
Bihar is not acting alone. Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh have already introduced similar curbs, signalling that state governments are increasingly willing to intervene where they believe subsidised fertiliser sales are being used to push other products. In Uttar Pradesh, the restrictions came into force on January 1, 2026, and cover non-subsidised products sold by major fertiliser suppliers. 
For policymakers, the appeal is straightforward: stop coercive selling and keep subsidised fertiliser distribution clean. For the industry, the worry is that a blunt restriction could also reduce availability of products that support precision farming, nutrient efficiency and long-term soil management. The tension between those two goals is likely to shape how other states respond if similar complaints surface in their markets. 
 What happens next will depend on whether Bihar chooses to refine the order or hold the line. If the state keeps the restrictions in place, fertiliser companies may have to redesign their channel strategy in a market where dealer networks remain central to farm input sales. If the government revisits the policy, the sector may get room to argue for a narrower solution that targets tagging without limiting access to newer nutrition technologies.

docs.title: India, Russia hold seventh round of talks on Pakistan and Afghanistan
docs.text:
India and Russia held the seventh round of talks under the India-Russia Special Mechanism on Pakistan and Afghanistan in New Delhi on Wednesday, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said.
 The meeting was co-chaired by India's Deputy National Security Adviser Pavan Kapoor and Russia's Deputy Secretary of the Security Council Aleksandr Venediktov .
Both sides held wide-ranging discussions on issues of common interest, including their impact on international security, the MEA said. 
They reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening ongoing cooperation under the India-Russia Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership.
During his visit, Venediktov also called on National Security Adviser Ajit Doval , according to the ministry.

 Shardiya Navratri 2026 will mark its fifth day on Thursday, October 15, when devotees will worship Maa Skandamata, the fifth form of Goddess Durga. Revered as the mother of Lord Kartikeya, also known as Skanda, the goddess symbolises maternal love, compassion, protection and spiritual strength. Devotees chant her sacred mantras during Navratri to seek peace, wisdom, family well-being and divine blessings.
 Maa Skandamata is traditionally depicted holding baby Kartikeya in her lap, with lotus flowers in her hands. Her serene appearance represents the nurturing and protective aspects of the Divine Mother. On this auspicious day, devotees perform puja, offer flowers and fruits, recite prayers and seek the goddess's blessings for themselves and their families.

Here are some important Maa Skandamata mantras, their meanings and the traditional ways to chant them on Navratri Day 5.
 Live Events
 Maa Skandamata Mantra for Navratri Day 5
The principal mantra associated with Maa Skandamata is a simple invocation that expresses devotion and reverence to the goddess.
 Mantra in Sanskrit: 
ॐ देवी स्कन्दमातायै नमः॥
 English transliteration: 
 Om Devi Skandamatayai Namah. 
 Meaning: I bow to Goddess Skandamata, the divine mother of Lord Skanda.
Devotees chant this mantra to express their faith in the goddess and seek her blessings for peace, courage, wisdom and harmony within the family. It is particularly significant on the fifth day of Navratri, which is dedicated to her worship. The mantra can be recited during morning puja or while meditating before the image of Maa Skandamata. Devotees may chant it 11, 21 or 108 times, according to their time, tradition and personal practice.
 Also Read: Happy Navratri Day 5 Wishes 2026: 50+ Maa Skandamata Quotes, Messages and WhatsApp Status 
 5 Important Maa Skandamata Mantras and Their Meanings
 1. Maa Skandamata Mool Mantra 
 Mantra: 
ॐ देवी स्कन्दमातायै नमः॥
 Transliteration: Om Devi Skandamatayai Namah.
 Meaning: Salutations to Goddess Skandamata, the mother of Lord Kartikeya.
 Significance: This is the main mantra devotees can use during their daily worship on Navratri Day 5. It represents surrender, devotion and a prayer for the goddess's grace. Devotees traditionally associate her worship with maternal protection, peace and family well-being.
 2. Maa Skandamata Prarthana Mantra 
 Mantra: 
सिंहासनगता नित्यं पद्माश्रितकरद्वया।
शुभदास्तु सदा देवी स्कन्दमाता यशस्विनी॥
 Transliteration: 
 Simhasanagata Nityam Padmashritakaradvaya, 
 Shubhadastu Sada Devi Skandamata Yashasvini. 
 Meaning: May the glorious Goddess Skandamata, seated upon her lion throne with lotuses in her hands, always bless her devotees with auspiciousness.
 Significance: This prayer praises the goddess's divine form and seeks her blessings for a positive and harmonious life. Devotees can recite it after the main mantra as part of their Navratri puja.
 3. Maa Skandamata Stuti Mantra 
 Mantra: 
या देवी सर्वभूतेषु माँ स्कन्दमाता रूपेण संस्थिता।
नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः॥
 Transliteration: 
 Ya Devi Sarvabhuteshu Maa Skandamata Rupena Samsthita, 
 Namastasyai Namastasyai Namastasyai Namo Namah. 
 Meaning: Salutations again and again to the Divine Goddess who resides among all beings in the form of Maa Skandamata.
 Significance: This devotional verse honours the goddess as a manifestation of divine feminine energy. Reciting it allows devotees to reflect on compassion, reverence and the sacred presence of the Divine Mother.
 4. Maa Skandamata Beej Mantra 
 Mantra: 
ॐ ह्रीं श्रीं स्कन्दमात्रै नमः॥
 Transliteration: Om Hreem Shreem Skandamatrai Namah.
 Meaning: A devotional invocation to Maa Skandamata using sacred seed syllables associated with divine energy and auspiciousness.
 Significance: Some devotional traditions use this mantra during more focused forms of goddess worship. As beej mantras can vary across traditions, devotees who follow a specific spiritual lineage may prefer the version taught by their guru or family tradition.
 5. Maa Durga Sarvamangala Mantra 
 Mantra: 
सर्वमङ्गलमाङ्गल्ये शिवे सर्वार्थसाधिके।
शरण्ये त्र्यम्बके गौरि नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते॥
 Transliteration: 
 Sarvamangala Mangalye Shive Sarvartha Sadhike, 
 Sharanye Tryambake Gauri Narayani Namostute. 
 Meaning: O Goddess, the most auspicious one, the benevolent fulfiller of worthy aspirations, the refuge of devotees and the divine Gauri, I bow to you.
 Significance: This widely recited hymn to the Goddess is suitable for Navratri worship. Devotees chant it to express gratitude, seek divine guidance and pray for well-being and auspiciousness.
 How to Chant Maa Skandamata Mantras on Navratri Day 5 
Devotees can follow a simple puja routine at home to worship Maa Skandamata on Thursday, October 15.
 Wake up and prepare for puja: Bathe, wear clean clothes and prepare a clean place for worship.
 Arrange the puja area: Place an image or idol of Maa Skandamata on a clean platform. If you are already observing Navratri puja, continue your established ritual.
 Light a diya: Light an oil or ghee lamp, if customary in your household, and offer prayers to the goddess.
 Offer flowers and prasad: Present flowers, fruits and other traditional offerings with devotion. Bananas are commonly offered to Maa Skandamata in Navratri traditions.
 Chant the main mantra: Recite “Om Devi Skandamatayai Namah” 11, 21 or 108 times. You may use a mala if that is part of your practi

Nifty ended Friday with sharp cuts amid selling pressure across the board, with consumer, IT and energy stocks dragging the markets the most. India VIX also moved back above its 200-DMA, indicating rising fear among the market participants. 
 Commenting on the technical charts, Rupak De, Senior Technical Analyst at LKP Securities, said that the setup has turned relatively cautious, with the index slipping below its 20-DMA for the first time in the past few sessions. Additionally, it has breached the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the prior up move from 24,571 to 26,341, he added. "With the index closing below the key support level of 25,500, the near-term bias appears weak, and there is potential for a decline toward the 25,000 mark in the short term. On the upside, immediate resistance is seen around 25,800," De said.
Here are 2 stock recommendations for Friday:
 Buy Kirloskar Oil Engines at Rs 1,375-1,385 | Upside: 5% | Target: Rs 1,500 | Stop Loss: Rs 1,320
 Kirloskar Oil Engines is currently taking a breakout of the rounding bottom formation on the daily time frame. The RSI is trending upward, reflecting positive momentum, and the stock finds support at the 21-day EMA, with all key EMAs rising. The stock is trading above important moving averages, indicating a bullish trend. 1,320 could work as an immediate support, and a hurdle can be seen at 1,500.
 (Drumil Vithlani, Technical Research Analyst, Bonanza Portfolio)

As preparations for the Union Budget 2026–27 gather pace, the groundwork underway signals a clear policy intent to accelerate domestic demand, revive private investment and generate employment, according to a budget note by Motilal Oswal Financial Services (MOFSL). The brokerage has identified five stocks across auto, agriculture, defence, financials and infrastructure themes, which it believes could deliver strong gains for investors.
 "The Budget is expected to focus on income-tax, GST, and customs simplification to enhance ease of doing business and support fiscal consolidation, alongside targeted support for agriculture, MSMEs, manufacturing, infrastructure, higher defence capex, EVs, and renewables through credit and incentives," the note authored by Research Analysts Sneha Poddar and Rekha Jaat said.
A strong capital expenditure thrust across highways, logistics, defence, rail freight corridors and connectivity is anticipated, complemented by emphasis on skilling, rural prosperity, women empowerment, AI adoption, climate action and digital finance to anchor India’s next phase of economic expansion, the note added.
The finance ministry started work on the Union Budget for 2026-27 from October 9 as per a circular issued by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA).
The preparations come against the backdrop of an additional 50% US tariff on most Indian goods and other external headwinds. These have raised risks to India's growth and jobs outlook, prompting calls for stronger support to the export sector.
 Live Events
 5 stocks to buy: 
The stocks recommended by MOFSL are TVS Motor Company, UPL , Bharat Dynamics (BDL), M&M Financial Services and Dalmia Bharat , and each of these stocks has been assigned a 20% weight.
 1) TVS Motors: TVS Motors continues to outperform peers and is well-positioned to benefit from the budget’s push to boost domestic consumption and rural demand through higher allocations, income support, and infrastructure spending.
MOFSL said that improving rural sentiment, strong entry-level recovery and sustained two-wheeler demand will be key triggers. Moreover, the company's market share gains, easing discounts, and margin expansion will provide strong earnings visibility. The Apache and Ntorq maker remains its top pick in OEMs.
 2) UPL: The diversified agrochemical leader is well positioned to benefit from the union budget push riding on rural prosperity via higher agri credit, MSME support, and value-chain strengthening, lifting farmer incomes and crop-protection demand.
The company's strong points are stronger volumes, export tailwinds, improved working-capital discipline and post-bond-repayment balance-sheet strength, the brokerage note said. The company's rising focus on speciality chemicals supports solid 2HFY26 growth.
 3) Bharat Dynamics: Bharat Dynamics (BDL), a defence play, has a robust Rs 50,000 crore order pipeline over five years, with Rs 20,000 crore targeted in 2-3 years. This aligns with the expected defence capex surge and infra push.
The recent Rs 2.5 lakh crore DAC approvals for missiles, undersea warfare, and naval arms leverage BDL's tactical/strategic expertise, propelling FY31 turnover to Rs 100bn via indigenisation and lower provisions, the note said.
 4) M&M Financial Services: M&M Financial is poised for Union Budget 2026-27 benefits via rural prosperity, MSME credit, and employment focus, driving PV/tractor loan growth amid surging volumes from festive demand, GST cuts, and restocking.
The company targets Rs 3 lakh crore in assets under management (AUM) by 2030, which is at an 18-20% CAGR, bolstered by AI underwriting, lower credit costs, controlled opex, and margin stability for strong earnings visibility in retail portfolios.
 5) Dalmia Bharat: The cement company benefits from the budget’s infra capex surge, PMAY rural housing, and urban projects, driving cement volume growth.
Dalmia Bharat is a low-cost cement producer with high blending ratios, green power and low freight. The company is targeting 62 mtpa capacity by FY28, and its cost optimisation endeavours will likely lift EBITDA margins amid sector consolidation.

Reliance Power 's board of directors on Monday approved the issuance of up to 46.20 crore equity shares/warrants worth Rs 1,525 crore via preferential allotment mode.
 The board has set the issue price at Rs 33 per share.
The issue price of equity shares/warrants is at a discount of 13% over Monday's closing price of Rs 38.15 on the NSE. The announcement was made after market hours and Reliance Power shares on Monday ended with gains of Rs 1.81 or 4.98% over the previous closing price.
 Reliance Infrastructure Limited, the promoter of the company, will enhance its equity stake by over Rs 600 crore, a company filing said. The other investors in the preferential issue are Authum Investment and Infrastructure Limited and Sanatan Financial Advisory Services Private Limited.
The proceeds from the preferential issue will be utilised to expand business operations directly and/or through investment in subsidiaries and joint ventures, debt reduction and for general corporate purposes, the filing said.

The markets worldwide are waiting with bated breath on what will be a historic policy announcement from the US Federal Reserve , where the central bank is expected to usher in a rate cut cycle.
 The announcement will be made at 11:30 pm IST (Indian Standard Time) on Wednesday.
If analysts are to be believed, the US Fed is all but certain to cut interest rates for the first time in more than four years.
However, there is no consensus on the quantum of reduction. Some are predicting a smaller cut of a quarter of a percentage point, while others believe a bigger half-point reduction is in the works.
Senior officials at the US central bank, including Powell, have indicated that a rate cut is coming, as inflation eases toward the bank's long-term target of 2%, and the labour market continues to cool in the post-Covid economy.
 Live Events
If the Fed starts the rate cut cycle, the Reserve Bank of India is also expected to follow suit.
A smaller cut would be a more predictable move, while a bigger cut would do more to boost demand — while also running the risk of reigniting inflation.
 WATCH LIVE TODAY: Press conference with #FOMC Chair Powell at 2:30 p.m. ET: https://t.co/1uJrua5qsH https://t.co/FJa6TbkDMt pic.twitter.com/87g5NJITsz 
— Federal Reserve (@federalreserve) September 18, 2024 
By the end 2024, markets are expecting a total reduction of at least 100 basis points in the first rate cut cycle in over 4 years since 2020.
But whether the Fed goes for 25 or 50 bps, the biggest trigger for stock prices to move up or down would be Powell's motivation behind the cut.
Asset classes from stocks, currencies and fixed income could all log swings in the immediate aftermath of the Fed decision.
While easing US interest rates are directionally positive for equities in general, “we should keep in mind interest rates are just one variable in a complex adaptive system that determines the direction of Indian equity markets”, said Anoop Vijaykumar, Investments and Head of Research at Capitalmind.

docs.text: Motilal Oswals research report on ICICI Prudential Life InsuranceICICI Prudential Life Insurance (IPRU) reported APE of INR28b (in line), reflecting growth of 16% YoY. For 1HFY27, APE grew 15% YoY, supported by strong 40% YoY growth in the protection business. VNB margin for the quarter stood at 25.4% vs our estimate of 25.5% and 24.5% in 2QFY26. For 1HFY27, VNB grew 22% YoY and VNB margin expanded 150bp YoY to 26%, backed by the product mix shift. For 2QFY27, IPRU’s shareholder PAT grew 27% YoY to INR3.7b. EV at the end of 1HFY27 was at INR566.7b, growing 12% YoY.  Rupak De, Senior Technical Analyst at LKP Securities 
Redington has reclaimed the 20EMA on the daily chart, indicating improving sentiment. The 20EMA and 50EMA are in a bullish crossover, while the stock is trading comfortably above the 200DMA, indicating a positive broader trend.
 Additionally, the hourly RSI is in a bullish crossover, suggesting improving momentum. Based on the chart setup, the trend is likely to remain strong in the coming days, with potential upside towards Rs 422. On the downside, support is placed at Rs 388, below which the stock could witness a deterioration in momentum.
Tata Technologies has broken out of a consolidation pattern on the daily chart, indicating improving sentiment. The price has been sustaining above the 20EMA, while the daily RSI is in a bullish crossover and continues to rise, suggesting strong momentum.
The short-term trend is likely to remain positive, with potential upside towards Rs 788. On the downside, support is placed at Rs 720, below which the stock could witness a sharp decline.
Canara Bank has reclaimed the 20EMA on the daily chart, indicating improving sentiment. It found support near a historical swing low before staging the current recovery.
Additionally, the daily RSI is in a bullish crossover and continues to rise, suggesting strengthening momentum. The short-term trend is likely to remain positive, with potential upside towards Rs 132. On the downside, support is placed at Rs 121.40, below which the stock could witness a sharp decline.
 Sudeep Shah, Head - Technical and Derivatives Research at SBI Securities 
Jindal Saw has broken out of its Rs 283–275 consolidation range that persisted since late September, closing higher and signalling an improvement in the near-term price structure. The chart structure suggests the potential for a fresh upward move. Over the next few trading sessions, Rs 1,660 will be a crucial level for the bulls. If the stock sustains above this level, the uptrend could extend towards Rs 1,840.
On the broader time frame, Hindustan Unilever had been in a prolonged downtrend. The stock has since staged a sharp recovery from oversold territory and its demand zone.
The chart structure and the RSI indicate that the current reversal could sustain, potentially marking the beginning of a new leg of the uptrend. For traders, Rs 1,810 is the key support level to watch. As long as the stock holds above this leve

 Fairfax to buy 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank for Rs 52,878 crore, announces govt
 The benchmark price used to evaluate qualified bids was Rs 81 per share, and the winning bid was higher than the benchmark price, the DIPAM secretary added.
 Moneycontrol News 
 October 14, 2026 / 18:35 IST 
 --> 
 According to government data, IDBI Bank's gross non-performing asset ratio declined from 31.78 percent in September 2018 to 2.32 percent in March 2026. 
 Cabinet approved IDBI Bank stake sale to Canada Inc.
 Govt and LIC to divest a combined 60.72% stake.
 The deal is worth more than 520 billion rupees.
 Did our AI summary help? 
 Market Mastery
Canada-based Fairfax Financial Holdings will acquire a majority stake in IDBI Bank after the government approved the lender’s strategic restructuring on Wednesday. The deal is valued at Rs 52,878 crore, Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said, making it one of the biggest foreign investments in India’s financial services sector.
Fairfax will offer Rs 81 per share, an 11% discount to IDBI Bank’s Wednesday closing price of Rs 90.40.
The Centre and state-run Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) will sell a combined 60.72% stake in the lender. The government will divest 30.48%, while LIC will sell 30.24%. Following the transaction, the government and LIC will retain a combined 34% stake in IDBI Bank.
“We need organisations that can meet growth capital for entrepreneurs,” Vaishnaw said while announcing the decision.
Read Also: Fairfax could bid $5 billion for IDBI Bank; said to offer to fully divest from CSB Bank 
The proposed sale was first announced in 2022 but faced regulatory and procedural delays. The process was put on hold in March after bids fell short of the government’s expected sale price.
According to the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) secretary, Rs 75.99 per share served as the benchmark price for evaluating qualified bids, and the winning bid exceeded that level.
On January 8, 2023, Moneycontrol was the first to report that Prem Watsa led Fairfax had submitted an EOI ( expression of interest ) for IDBI Bank.
The share purchase agreement is expected to be signed and executed before the end of the current calendar year. The invested capital will remain locked in for three years, and IDBI Bank will retain its existing brand name, the DIPAM secretary said.
LIC will have to reduce its stake in IDBI Bank to 15% within two years, in line with Reserve Bank of India (RBI) norms.
The approved buyer, Canada Inc, whose parent entity is Fairfax Financial Holdings, will submit its credentials to the RBI under the ‘fit and proper’ assessment completed at the Expression of Interest (EoI) stage. It will also submit a roadmap for complying with regulatory conditions, the DIPAM secretary said.
On July 13, 2026 Moneycontrol first reported that alongside two CGD meetings, an Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) also met on July 13 to take stock of the strategic disinvestment of IDBI Bank.
The valuation considered both tangible and intangible assets, including land and properties, along with liabilities, the secretary added.
Under RBI norms, Canada Inc will have to decide whether to merge CSB Bank with IDBI Bank or sell its stake in CSB Bank within two years of the execution of the share purchase agreement.
“The government continues to stay invested in IDBI. We still have a 15% stake,” the Finance Minister said.

 Stock market recap: Benchmark stock indices Sensex and Nifty closed lower on Wednesday as investors booked profits after a sharp rally in the previous session, while a spike in wholesale price inflation and firm crude oil prices weighed on sentiment.

 The 50-share NSE Nifty declined 99.25 points, or 0.44%, to close at 22,622.70.
 Among the 30 Sensex constituents, Bajaj Finance, Mahindra & Mahindra, Bajaj Finserv, Eternal, ICICI Bank and InterGlobe Aviation were among the major laggards.
 Infosys, Tech Mahindra, Tata Consultancy Services, Hindustan Unilever, NTPC and Reliance Industries were among the major gainers.
 Two stock recommendations by MarketSmith India: 
 Buy: Jindal Saw Ltd (current price: ₹ 297) 
 Why it’s recommended: Strong water infrastructure and Jal Jeevan Mission-led demand is driving robust growth in the high-margin ductile iron (DI) pipe business. A healthy domestic and export pipeline order book provides multi-year revenue visibility across water, oil & gas, and infrastructure projects. 
 Key metrics: P/E: 30.14, 52-week high: ₹ 320.00, volume: ₹ 84.20 crore

 Risk factors: Dependence on government and EPC-led projects exposes the company to order delays and payment of collection risks. Volatility in steel prices and geopolitical disruptions in export markets can impact margins and execution. 
 Buy: ₹ 294–298

 Buy: Shyam Metalics and Energy Ltd (current price: ₹ 1,141) 
 Why it’s recommended: Large ongoing capex in stainless steel, aluminium, and value-added products is expected to drive strong earnings growth over the next few years. Backward integration and captive power facilities provide a structural cost advantage and support profitability. 
 Key metrics: P/E: 27.35, 52-week high: ₹ 1,148.00, volume: ₹ 53.67 crore

This is an early bullish crossover, although both lines remain deep in negative territory.

docs.title: Defence stocks to buy: HAL, Bharat Dynamics, MIDHANI are DAM Capital's top picks with up to 39% upside - check targets
docs.text:
Brokerage DAM Capital, following discussions with industry leaders and management teams, has identified Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL), Mishra Dhatu Nigam (MIDHANI) and Bharat Dynamics (BDL) as its preferred picks among defence public sector undertakings (DPSUs). It also sees opportunities in private-sector companies Astra Microwave Products and Zen Technologies. In a recent report, DAM Capital said the sector was moving beyond an order-driven expansion phase towards growth led by technology, capabilities and manufacturing capacity. A pipeline of major defence procurement programmes awaiting final approvals could provide additional visibility for companies supplying aircraft, submarines, missile systems and associated components. HAL remains DAM Capital's top pick among DPSUs, followed by MIDHANI and BDL, reflecting their respective positions in aircraft, specialised aerospace materials and missile systems. Bharat Dynamics : For BDL, DAM Capital listed a target price of ₹ 1,560, indicating an upside potential of 39%. The company had an order book of approximately ₹ 261.8 billion at the end of FY26, providing four to five years of execution visibility. Its near-term pipeline includes QRSAM, heavyweight torpedoes and air-to-air missiles. The brokerage also highlighted BDL's efforts to improve execution after technical issues and supplier-quality problems affected deliveries in FY26. DAM Capital said in its report: "BDL is entering a strong execution phase, with FY27 revenue targeted at ~ ₹ 55bn and a longer-term goal of ₹ 100bn by FY30, supported by a robust ~ ₹ 262bn order book providing 4–5 years of visibility and a ~ ₹ 150bn near-term pipeline across QRSAM, heavyweight torpedoes and air-to-air missiles." Hindustan Unilever : For HAL, the brokerage report listed a target price of ₹ 5,940, indicating an upside potential of 22%. The company's Tejas Mk1A programme is approaching the final stages before induction, although radar and missile integration issues and final regulatory clearance remain important milestones. The report noted that HAL had 27 Tejas Mk1A airframes ready, with 10 GE F404 engines received and four more in transit at the time of the assessment. Beyond Tejas, HAL's growth opportunities include the HTT-40 trainer, Dhruv NG helicopters, the CATS Warrior programme and the proposed LCA LIFT trainer. Expanding engine manufacturing capacity could also help support production over the medium term. Mishra Dhatu Nigam : MIDHANI, meanwhile, is positioned to benefit from rising demand for titanium alloys, superalloys and specialised steels used in fighter aircraft, aero-engines, space and naval platforms. The report listed a target price of ₹ 475, implying an over 8% potential upside. Its opportunities include import substitution, aerospace certifications, modernisation spending and potential orders from global aerospace manufacturers. DAM Capital noted: “MIDHANI is well positioned for sustained growth, supported by its strong competitive moat in strategic materials, expanding aerospace and defence applications and rising import-substitution opportunities. The company’s integrated capabilities across superalloys, titanium alloys and special steels, 500+ grades, stringent customer qualification requirements and advanced manufacturing infrastructure create high entry barriers.” DAM Capital sees defence electronics as a structural growth opportunity, with the market expected to grow at over 15% CAGR over the medium term, driven by domestic production, import substitution and exports. The brokerage favours Astra Microwave Products and Zen Technologies, given their exposure to radar, electronic warfare, counter-drone and simulation technologies. Solar Industries remains on its watchlist following its recent acquisition. Drones are another growth driver, with a proposed ₹ 200 billion Fast Track Procurement programme covering unmanned aerial vehicles, loitering munitions and surveillance systems. Deliveries could begin over the next 18–24 months. DAM Capital said: “The defence procurement pipeline remains a key medium-term order catalyst, with several large-ticket programmes across the three services awaiting CCS approval/final government clearance.” The brokerage estimates that proposed programmes, including 114 Rafale fighters, six P-75(I) submarines, eight Next Generation Corvettes and QRSAM, represent a potential ₹ 5 trillion order opportunity. Rising aerospace capital expenditure, exports and global partnerships could further support growth, although approvals, execution and margins remain key risks. docs.title: Hero Motors share price jumps 6.5% on strong Q2 results | Check share price performance, earnings details | Buy or sell?
docs.text:
Hero Motors shares opened at ₹ 161 per share on NSE today, as compared to previous close of ₹ 155.19 on Tuesday and touched an intraday high of ₹ 167.39 on 14 October.
The stock has, which made its stock market debut on 23 September, has fallen 3.5% in a week, however, has gained 67.47% on year-to-date (YTD) basis.
Auto components manufacturer Hero Motors, on Tuesday, reported a net profit of ₹ 10.2 crore for the second quarter, more than doubling from ₹ 4.73 crore in the same period last year. Revenue rose 24.9% year-on-year to ₹ 319.3 crore, compared with ₹ 255.7 crore in the year-ago quarter.
The company’s earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) jumped 92% year-on-year to ₹ 35.9 crore from ₹ 18.7 crore. Its EBITDA margin also improved to 11.3% in the quarter from 7.3% a year earlier.
Separately, Hero Motors has proposed acquiring an additional 39% stake in its subsidiary, Hewland Engineering Ltd (HEL), from existing shareholders William Hewland and Siobhan Hewland for approximately £0.60 million in cash. The transaction covers 8,039 equity shares with a face value of £1 each and will increase Hero Motors’ stake in HEL from 51% to 90%. The acquisition is expected to be completed within around six months and does not require any governmental or regulatory approvals.
Hero Motors is an automotive technology company engaged in designing, developing, manufacturing and supplying powertrain solutions to automotive original equipment manufacturers across the US, Europe, India and the ASEAN region. Its product portfolio caters to two-wheelers, electric bicycles, off-road vehicles, electric and hybrid cars, and heavy-duty vehicles. The company’s customers include BMW, Ducati, Enviolo, Formula Motorsport, Hummingbird EV and HWA.

docs.title: How to invest when your income doesn’t arrive every month
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 How to invest when your income doesn’t arrive every month
 Rahul Mehra 4 min read 14 Oct 2026, 11:01 AM IST 
 Summary
 For freelancers and business owners, irregular cash flows can make monthly SIPs difficult to sustain. An annual investment target, fixed asset allocation and adequate liquidity can help. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The first piece of advice almost every new investor receives is the same: start a systematic investment plan (SIP), pick a date and let it run. It is sound advice. But it also quietly assumes something many people do not have: a paycheque that arrives on the same day every month.
 Freelancers, consultants, traders and small business owners all deal with income that does not follow a fixed schedule. Some months are busy, others are lean, and a single large invoice can arrive a quarter late. For them, the standard monthly-SIP playbook is not just difficult to follow; it is built on a foundation they do not have.
 So what should investing look like when income itself is irregular?
 Think in years, not months 
 The mistake is to treat the SIP as the goal rather than a tool. For someone on a fixed salary, a missed SIP may be a lapse in discipline. For someone with uneven income, missing an SIP in a lean month is often unavoidable. The guilt of missing it is what can break the habit altogether.
 The fix is to change the unit of planning. Instead of committing a fixed sum on a fixed date, decide how much you intend to invest over a full year and deploy it whenever money actually arrives. A strong month funds more; a weak month funds less or nothing, without any sense of failure.
 The discipline shifts from “invest every month” to “invest every rupee that is surplus, as it comes in”. That is a target an irregular earner can realistically meet.
 Fix the allocation
 The harder problem with lumpy income is not how much to invest but where to put it each time a payment clears. Answering that question afresh every time invites second-guessing and, worse, the temptation to chase whatever has recently performed well.
 A fixed asset allocation removes the guesswork. A simple model, say 60% equity, 30% debt and 10% gold, means that when money arrives, you already know where it goes. You are topping up a plan, not making a fresh investment call.
 This matters particularly for irregular earners because their opportunities to invest come in bursts, often when markets are doing something dramatic.
 Liquidity first
 For someone with a steady salary, the standard advice is to maintain an emergency fund covering about six months of expenses. For someone without a regular paycheque, that buffer needs to be larger, closer to nine to twelve months.
 The reason is straightforward. If a lean stretch coincides with a market fall and you have no cushion, you may be forced to sell equities at exactly the wrong time to pay the bills. That single forced sale can undo years of patient investing.
 So build the emergency fund and debt allocation first, then feed the equity portfolio once that financial floor is in place. Returns are what you pursue after securing liquidity, not before.
 Handle the good months 
 The lean months are not the real danger. The good months are.
 When a large payment lands, the natural urge is to put it straight into whichever asset or sector has rallied the most recently. It feels like making up for lost time. In practice, this is how investors buy at peaks and regret it later.
 A fixed allocation provides the discipline to resist that impulse. A large inflow gets split in the same way as a small one, across equity, debt and gold in the proportions already decided, rather than being poured into the theme of the moment.
 Investing, in the end, is mostly about making fewer mistakes. A plan decided in a calm moment protects you from the decisions you might otherwise make in an excited one.
 Keep things simple
 None of this requires a complicated portfolio, especially if you are investing on your own, without an intermediary’s guidance.
 Passive index funds can form the core of a portfolio, reducing confusion and the temptation to keep switching schemes. Active funds can potentially outperform their benchmark indices, but choosing them requires a better understanding of the fund manager’s track record across market cycles.
 For the debt allocation, investors can consider shorter-duration funds, where interest-rate sensitivity is lower, as well as categories such as corporate bond funds or banking and PSU funds. For the gold allocation, a simple gold ETF can be considered.
 Rahul Mehra is a Mumbai-based mutual fund distributor.

docs.title: Who regulates the regulator?
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 Who regulates the regulator?
 Suresh Mathur 4 min read 14 Oct 2026, 12:50 PM IST 
 Summary
 India needs strong insurance regulation, but interventions must be judged by their impact on coverage, claims and consumer outcomes. Irdai should correct market failures without prescribing commercial choices. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 India needs strong insurance regulation. Solvency, governance, consumer protection and disclosure require a firm regulatory hand, and Irdai has helped build a stronger, more policyholder-oriented market. But effective regulation also requires restraint, measurement and accountability for outcomes.
 An important distinction deserves attention: the difference between regulating a market and designing it. A regulator must intervene against mis-selling, weak governance and threats to policyholders. But should it also decide what products should look like, how they should be distributed or how sophisticated market participants should transact? The closer regulation moves towards product design, pricing, distribution and commercial economics, the greater the risk of distorting market outcomes.
 Markets have a feedback loop; regulation often does not. If an insurer launches a product customers do not want, it loses money. If an intermediary overcharges, customers may move elsewhere.
 Once a regulatory solution is prescribed, however, the industry must implement it. Technology is built, products are modified and processes are changed. If an intervention creates unintended consequences, there is no equivalent mechanism to ensure its withdrawal. The regulated are accountable for their decisions; regulation should be equally accountable for its outcomes.
 That suggests a simple test: what problem was the intervention intended to solve, what outcome was expected, and did it materialise? Compliance alone is not success. Adoption, customer behaviour, coverage and consumer outcomes matter.
 Measure the impact
 Regulation must be judged by outcomes, not intent. Bima Vahak aimed to expand insurance through a localized, women-centric distribution network. But success must be measured by customers reached, policies sold and renewed, and coverage added, not merely by the programme’s launch.
 Similarly, Bharat Sookshma & Laghu Udyam Suraksha sought to simplify insurance through standardized products. The real test is whether these products improved access and brought more people into the insurance market. A policy introduced is not a problem solved; compliance is not impact.
 What share of the previously uninsured did these products bring into the market? Did they improve first-time ownership or persistency? If the objective was wider coverage, those are the metrics that matter.
 The underlying assumption may have been that complexity was a major barrier. But affordability is only one factor. Trust, distribution, awareness, claims experience and perceived value matter too. A standard product can make comparison easier without necessarily improving access.
 Target market failures 
 There is a strong case for intervention where data shows a persistent market failure. In FY2024–25, 258,000 grievances were reported through Bima Bharosa, up from 216,000 the previous year. Of these, 137,000 related to general and health insurance, and 69% of general-insurance grievances were claim-related. Life-insurance grievances also highlighted concerns around unfair business practices, policy servicing and claims.
 These are areas where intervention has a clear rationale. The problem is visible, measurable and directly connected to policyholder outcomes. Where claims are not settled, products are mis-sold or disclosure is inadequate, the regulator is correcting a market failure.
 The case for prescription is weaker in commercial decisions. Before intervening, the question should be where the market failure lies. If there is mis-selling , strengthen conduct supervision. If customers lack information, improve disclosure. If competition is weak, address barriers to competition.
 Where informed customers have choices and multiple providers compete, prescription should be cautious. Can the market solve the problem without it?
 Grow the market
 There is a broader reason for restraint. India’s insurance market remains significantly underpenetrated. Overall penetration was 3.7% of GDP in FY2024–25, with life at 2.7% and non-life at just 1%. Insurance density improved only from $95 to $97.
 India needs not only a better-regulated market, but a much larger one.
 The sector issued 418.4 million policies, collected ₹ 11.93 trillion in premiums and paid ₹ 8.36 trillion in claims during FY2024–25. These numbers show both the scale of the system and the millions of customer interactions that regulation ultimately affects.
 That makes outcome measurement even more important. For every major intervention, the regulator should ask: Did coverage increase? Did customer choice improve? Did complaints fall? Did claims outcomes improve? Did costs fall without reducing access? Did competition increase? And were there unintended consequences?
 If the answer is no, regulation should be capable of being reviewed, amended or withdrawn.
 That is not an argument for weaker regulation. It is an argument for better regulation.
 Strong regulation is not regulation that controls more of the market. It is regulation that knows where control creates value and where restraint creates value.
 The regulator should regulate the market. It should not design the market.
 Suresh Mathur, former executive director at the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai).

Global 
 America’s election officials are ready for trouble
 The Economist 5 min read 14 Oct 2026, 08:38 PM IST 
 Summary
 Election experts’ nightmare scenario is that Mr Trump might try to seize voting equipment or ballots. That would break the “chain of custody”, the controls that set out who can handle ballots and where they go, ensuring all are accounted for. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 On a fine day in Florence, a city an hour’s drive from Phoenix, staff at the local voting centre are doing a tabletop exercise, the euphemism to describe training for election hell. The point is to imagine calamities—fire, power outages, bomb threats—then have a Plan B, C and D. Officials have always made some doomsday preparations, but this year’s exercise is more thorough, and the range of threats broader. What, for example, should they do if federal law-enforcement agents show up at the polls?
 The staff run through the protocols. Monitors from the Department of Justice (DoJ) can stay if they have an official letter, and indeed the government has said 1,000 will be dispatched across the country. Any other agents must vacate unless they are themselves voting; Arizona law mandates a perimeter of 75 feet (25 metres) around precincts. “If they refuse to leave, that’s when the scenario becomes a scenario,” says an election worker in the recorder’s office in Pinal county, of which Florence is the seat. In other words: call the sheriff.
 Pinal is a Republican county. A portion of it lies in Arizona’s 6th congressional district, one of several dozen competitive House races in the midterm elections on November 3rd. Our forecast suggests Democrats will flip the House and possibly the Senate, too. The nagging question is what schemes, if any, Donald Trump might attempt to subvert the election’s legitimate results.
 His effort to overturn his loss in 2020 wisened up everyone to the many pressure points in America’s decentralised election system, and the lengths he might go to squeeze them. So far, his many attempted interventions this year have amounted to little, with Congress and the Supreme Court blocking his efforts to rewrite voting procedures. States, not the federal government, run elections; and their rules are mostly unchanged from past cycles. However the executive branch has shifted from being a force to support elections’ integrity to one undermining it, and in November the system will be tested once more.
 Some changes represent not active interference, but the removal of help. Last year the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) stopped covering localities’ cost to participate in a service for sharing cyber threats. Membership in the programme is down by two-thirds. The upshot is that cyberattacks are more likely to proliferate, says Geoff Hale, formerly of CISA. “If a jurisdiction faces one and gets compromised or repels it, but if they’re not sharing information about that attack, then other election jurisdictions remain equally vulnerable.” Similarly, the FBI reportedly has no plans to stand up its election command centre, which in past years monitored threats and co-ordinated with local law enforcement.
 However, election administrators increasingly view the feds as a threat, too, says Jonathan Miller of Public Rights Project (PRP), a litigation group that represents local governments. Earlier this year the DoJ said it would prosecute officials who let non-citizens vote. Such voter fraud is extremely rare, but the spectre of non-citizen voting propels the myth of election theft. It is the reason that MAGA activists say they want immigration enforcement at the polls.
 Their presence would be illegal: federal law prohibits government officials from sending armed agents to precincts. On behalf of the city of Denver, PRP has sued the Department of Homeland Security, seeking to pre-empt anything like that on election day. The Trump administration says it has no intention to patrol precincts, but that it may take targeted action, such as serving warrants against anyone suspected of being an illegal immigrant. Democrats fear that an enforcement presence near polling places would dampen turnout by minorities, who tend to vote Democratic. In a survey by UC San Diego, a third of Hispanics said they anticipate being questioned at the polls despite being citizens. Nearly half say they expect some form of intimidation.
 Election experts’ nightmare scenario is that Mr Trump might try to seize voting equipment or ballots. That would break the “chain of custody”, the controls that set out who can handle ballots and where they go, ensuring all are accounted for. Losing custody would make it hard to know whether ballots had been manipulated. “I would feel very uncomfortable about validating those ballots,” says Stephen Richer, a former recorder in Arizona’s Maricopa county. “Then you start going down the dark road of, like, do you have to call a new election?”
 Two incidents concerning past elections have primed Democrats to the possibility of meddling. In January the FBI raided an election office in Fulton county, Georgia, and carted away material from 2020. Then in March, Chad Bianco, a Republican sheriff in Riverside, California, seized ballots that had been cast in a statewide referendum last year. Both the FBI and Mr Bianco cited misinformation in their requests for warrants.
 Could there be a similar ruse in November? The prior incidents occurred after elections were over, not in the middle of one. This month Mr Trump welcomed Tina Peters at the White House. A former county clerk, she went to prison for giving a fellow election denier unauthorised access to voting machines in 2020, then was pardoned by Colorado’s Democratic governor. On her visit to Washington, she reportedly pitched Mr Trump on a plan to seize ballots this November. Ed Martin, another MAGA troublemaker who d

docs.title: Israel’s election overseer on how to stop AI distorting votes
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Israel’s election overseer on how to stop AI distorting votes
 The Economist 4 min read 14 Oct 2026, 08:29 PM IST 
 Summary
 The danger need not begin with malicious intent. A model may draw on stale information, favour popular viewpoints or give different answers to similar questions. In 2025 the Dutch data-protection authority warned that chatbots gave distorted voting advice. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 A RELATIVE OF mine recently consulted an AI chatbot about which of the dishes his mother had prepared he should eat. I pointed out that he ate her cooking every week, whereas the chatbot had never tasted it. He replied that he consulted the chatbot about everything. Apparently, having no taste buds was no obstacle to becoming the family’s food critic.
 The exchange was amusing. Its implications for my work are less so. As interim head of the Israeli Central Elections Committee, I am preparing for our parliamentary election on October 27th. AI companies should use the time remaining to address a question that reaches far beyond Israel: what happens when “What should I eat?” becomes “Who should I vote for?”
 Chatbots can make politics easier to understand. They can explain electoral systems, make sense of manifestos and help citizens interrogate competing claims. Those benefits matter.
 But a voting recommendation involves judgments about values, credibility and trade-offs. Presenting it as the personalised output of an apparently impartial machine can conceal the assumptions that produced it.
 The danger need not begin with malicious intent. A model may draw on stale information, favour popular viewpoints or give different answers to similar questions. In 2025 the Dutch data-protection authority warned that chatbots gave distorted voting advice, repeatedly favouring two parties, sometimes despite users’ stated preferences. Research published in Nature found that models instructed to advocate particular candidates could shift participants’ preferences. That shows persuasive capacity, not that ordinary chatbot use has changed an election result.
 Malicious actors introduce another risk. They can plant misleading material in sources that AI systems retrieve, hoping to have propaganda delivered in the reassuring voice of an assistant. Demos, a British think-tank, has documented leading AI services amplifying narratives from a Russian influence operation. An attacker need not control the model if they can contaminate its information supply.
 For the voter, the author of that intervention may be invisible. A campaign leaflet announces its allegiance; an answer from a familiar chatbot can feel like disinterested advice from someone who knows you. The trust earned through hundreds of mundane exchanges can carry across into a decision with public consequences.
 To the companies building these systems, I propose five commitments.
 First, decline to recommend people vote one way or another, including through party rankings or purported compatibility scores. Explain policies and compare verifiable positions using clear criteria, while leaving the judgment to the voter.
 Brazil’s electoral court has already banned AI providers from recommending or ranking candidates and parties, even when users ask them to do it. Companies should adopt this principle wherever they operate. Factual comparison and robust political discussion should remain available. Companies should publish the boundary clearly, so a safeguard for voter autonomy does not become an excuse to suppress inconvenient questions or criticism.
 Second, make election information verifiable. Questions about eligibility, polling places, procedures and results should draw on current sources from the responsible electoral authorities, with links users can inspect. Political claims require clearly attributed sources and visible uncertainty. A party’s promise should be identified as merely a promise. Where reliable information is unavailable, the system should say so.
 Third, defend the sources as well as the model. Detect co-ordinated attempts to flood retrieval systems. Check provenance. Avoid treating repetition across copied websites as independent corroboration. Establish rapid channels with election authorities and independent researchers to investigate errors and manipulation. Corrections must be made while voters can still use them.
 Fourth, keep personalisation from becoming political profiling. Information entrusted to an assistant about someone’s finances, health or anxieties should never become material for steering their vote. Companies should explicitly prohibit using conversational memory or inferred vulnerabilities for electoral persuasion.
 Fifth, make safeguards testable. Publish election-specific evaluations, disclose material failures and give independent researchers meaningful access under privacy protections. Test repeated conversations and attempts to evade restrictions. In Israel, that means checking Hebrew, Arabic, Russian and English. A promise of neutrality is inadequate without evidence that the safeguards work across languages and political viewpoints.
 Election officials must provide clear information. Citizens must exercise judgment. Companies, however, control the systems through which that judgment is increasingly formed. Asking them to preserve voters’ autonomy is a practical condition for public trust. They should publish and follow through on these commitments before polling day, with named teams accountable for delivery.
 My relative can return to his mother’s table next week and reconsider the chatbot’s culinary advice. An election offers no such weekly correction. AI should help citizens understand their choices. The choice itself must remain theirs.

 Festive hiring to rise 10-15% despite consumption woes, bonuses may shrink
 Vaeshnavi Kasthuril , Devina Sengupta 5 min read 15 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 Weak consumption, inflation, and pricier gadgets cloud hopes for sales. Flipkart and Amazon are expanding seasonal roles, but abundant labour and soft demand may keep bonuses largely flat. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 India’s biggest hiring season is here, but a consumption slowdown is clouding the outlook for festive recruitment in the organized sector.
 Yet seasonal hiring of contract and gig workers is expected to rise by 10-15% year-on-year, staffing agencies say, as e-commerce, consumer, logistics and auto companies pull out all the stops to drive sales amid a weak monsoon, inflation and tighter household budgets.
 Seasonal hiring by two of India’s largest e-commerce players offers evidence. Flipkart said it had increased festive-season job opportunities to more than 250,000, from over 220,000 in 2025. Rival Amazon India said it had created more than 160,000 seasonal job opportunities across its e-commerce and quick-commerce operations, up from over 150,000 in August 2025.
 However, performance-linked incentives for these additional workers may be muted, reflecting uncertainty over how strongly sales will pick up.
 “The drought will cause more agricultural workers to move to the metros, since the impact will be felt mostly in the rural belts. This will increase the availability of workers, and we see a 10-15% rise in demand this festive period compared to last year,” said Sunil Chemmankotil, country manager, human resources and workforce solutions company Adecco India.
 Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka have already declared drought conditions amid El Niño, a climate pattern marked by warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean.
 Typically, consumer -facing firms hire workers across metros, smaller cities and rural areas during the festive season. But water scarcity could push more workers towards cities in search of short-term jobs, keeping labour supply ample and limiting the need for higher payouts.
 “The bonuses and performance-linked payouts will remain similar to last year because companies will see a sufficient supply of workforce in the delivery, logistics, e-commerce, and retail sectors, which hire staffing during this period,” said Chemmankotil.
 Consumption blues
 Temporary workers are hired through third-party vendors and deployed at client sites for three to six months. Gig workers, typically in delivery services, may work for multiple companies. Both are in demand during India’s festive season, which begins around September and peaks in October-November around Diwali.
 Staffing firms begin hiring months in advance to help manufacturers, automakers and electronics companies prepare for the sales rush. Demand for gig workers , meanwhile, peaks during the festive period as delivery volumes rise.
 “Around Dussehra, if you find that customers are buoyant and demand has picked up, then that’s great. But we can’t tell now for sure,” said A. Balasubramanian, senior vice-president at staffing firm TeamLease.
 Similarly, workers move to urban areas and nearby towns for seasonal work during the festive period, then return to their farms towards the end of November. “Now there could be an additional spike, simply because work is even less now,” he said, referring to the possibility that farm distress could push more workers to seek jobs outside agriculture.
 Kartik Narayan, chief executive of online jobs marketplace Apna, noted that in smaller towns, where delivery volumes may be lower, workers may be less willing to take jobs without assured earnings, unlike in larger cities, where shipments are usually higher.
 The additional hiring comes amid mounting pressure on household budgets from rising inflation. Retail inflation accelerated to 5.54% in September, nearing the Reserve Bank of India’s 6% upper tolerance limit. The central bank raised its repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% on 7 October, adding to pressure on household finances.
 Economists noted that 2025’s goods and services tax (GST) overhaul, which cut taxes on passenger vehicles, two-wheelers and premium consumer durables to 18% from 28%, unlocked pent-up demand across income groups, aided by easy credit availability. Discretionary spending among urban middle- and lower-income households has since held up in the first half of the current fiscal year despite rising inflation.
 But experts warn that the momentum may fade after the festive season , as a weaker monsoon threatens farm activity and rural demand, while car, electronics, and home prices keep rising, Mint reported on 29 September.
 Mint reported on 7 October that though input costs for most home and kitchen goods remain stable, they are rising for appliances, the segment’s largest by value. While major manufacturers are trying to hold back price hikes, companies have been raising prices across product portfolios. Smartphones, a key festive-season purchase, are also expected to see their steepest sales decline in a decade as memory chips become costlier, Mint reported on 17 September.
 TeamLease also pointed out that September was not a good month for several consumer-facing companies, including those selling consumables and appliances. Overall consumption could be weaker than expected, A. Balasubramanian cautioned.
 Flat wages 
 Recruiters said roles in picking, packing, shipping and delivery would pay ₹ 25,000- ₹ 50,000, including incentives, with compensation largely unchanged across most roles.
 The Indian Staffing Federation (ISF) explained to Mint how jobs are split between the gig and staffing sectors. Gig work is attractive for its flexibility and low skill entry barriers as a first job. While logistics teams are now hiring gig workers, tho

 Own a house in another city? Here’s what it costs to manage it
 Shipra Singh 7 min read 14 Oct 2026, 03:33 PM IST 
 Summary
 Remote property owners can outsource vacation-rental operations or long-term tenancy management, but these services and fees come at a high cost. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 For non-resident Indians (NRIs) and people who own a house in another city, managing a property remotely can be challenging. Tenants may default on rent, urgent repairs may be needed, or a house may remain vacant for months. Property management companies offer to handle these responsibilities for a fee. 
 These services are broadly offered in two forms. The first involves converting and managing a property as a bed and breakfast (BnB) or guest house for short-term rentals. This can be useful for second-home owners who visit occasionally and want to earn rental income while ensuring the property is maintained in their absence. 
 The second involves end-to-end management of conventional long-term rentals–from finding tenants and collecting rent to handling repairs and tenant-related issues–without requiring the landlord's regular involvement. 
 However, these services come at a high cost. Owners need to weigh the fees against the convenience of outsourcing property management and the rental income they can expect to earn. 
 What is offered? 
 In the first category, short-term rental management companies take over the day-to-day operations of running a property as a BnB or guest house. They list the property on platforms such as Airbnb, MakeMyTrip and Booking.com, set nightly tariffs, manage reservations, coordinate guest check-ins and check-outs, and oversee housekeeping, caretakers and maintenance. They also handle guest complaints and provide owners with booking and earnings reports. 
 The scope of services differs across agencies and packages they offer. Ethan Barman, founder, Hostizzy, a vacation rental management company, said they offer a choice between one-time setup, co-hosting and complete management. 
 “In the first option, we get the property listed and priced, and the owner runs it themselves. In the other two packages, we take over housekeeping, guest management and on-ground supervision as well, including adjusting pricing with demand, weekend and festivals, and revenue sharing ranges from 15%-30% depending on the range of services the owner signs up for.” 
 Most vacation rental management companies work on similar models. Gaurav Marwah, co-founder and director of VacationBuddy, another vacation property management company, said the company also handles property photography, marketing and owner reporting, apart from day-to-day operations. 
 For conventional long-term rentals, the scope of services differs, with the company's involvement largely limited to managing the tenancy and property maintenance. This includes finding tenants, conducting background checks, completing paperwork, handling tenant queries and ensuring timely rent collection. At the end of the tenancy, the company oversees the handover, assesses damage and helps settle security deposits. 
 Pryank Agarwal, founder and CEO of Housewise, which manages long-term rentals, says the service is designed for owners who live away from their properties and need dependable local assistance. “We represent the owner in a tenancy, so that they don’t have to be involved. Every maintenance or society-related issue, major or minor, is handled by us,” he said. 
 To be sure, while the company does the ground work, it does not pay for actual repairs. “The cost is attributed to either the owner or the tenant, depending on the situation–the tenant pays if they’ve caused the damage, whereas the owner covers for structural issues or major repairs arising from the age of the property. But we manage the entire process on behalf of the owner, right from inspection, quote, cost attribution and ensuring the repair is done properly,” said Agarwal. 
 Know the cost 
 Long-term rental management companies charge either a fixed fee or a percentage of monthly rent. Housewise charges 1.25 times the monthly rent for a one-year agreement. For a house rented at ₹ 30,000 a month, the annual fee works out to ₹ 37,500, or 10.4% of the annual rental income. PropertyAngel charges 9% of monthly rent, while NoBroker offers property management packages at fixed fees ranging from ₹ 18,000 to ₹ 29,999. 
 Short-term rental management costs more as properties require attention after every guest stay. Most companies follow a revenue-sharing model for full end-to-end services, while some, such as BlueLeaf, offer guaranteed monthly payouts. 
 In revenue sharing, companies charge around 30% of booking revenue, net of commissions charged by the listing platform. Additional charges may also apply. For instance, VacationBuddy charges a one-time onboarding fee of ₹ 11,000–21,000 for property photography, social media promotions and other marketing activities. 
 Owners who don't want to hand over complete operations can opt for cheaper listing-only or co-hosting services. Hostizzy charges upwards of ₹ 14,999 as a one-time fee to list and price the property, after which the owner manages it. Its co-hosting services cost ₹ 15,000–40,000 a month or 10–17% of revenue. "Our most popular plan is 18% of net revenue (booking value minus OTA commission) and includes a direct booking website for the property," said Barman. OTA is online travel aggregators. 
 Owners should check whether the management fee is calculated on gross booking revenue or after deducting platform commissions, as this can significantly affect their earnings.
